stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Renata Villacorta's 2011 novel The Fourth Morning. Ines, a linguist, is recording Aldo, one of the last fluent speakers of a mountain dialect.

For three mornings Ines had arrived with her printed lists (every pronoun, every tense, every way to say carry), and for three mornings Aldo had answered each prompt with a story about his brother or a stubborn mule. She had begun marking those minutes in her notebook as lost. On the fourth morning, however, transcribing the tale of the mule, she found in it four tenses her lists had never thought to ask for. After that she left the lists in her bag and simply asked him what happened next.
choices: To portray a speaker's reluctance to answer a researcher's questions until he comes to trust her
To show a researcher giving up her scholarly aims so that she can simply enjoy a speaker's stories
To depict a researcher realizing that what she had written off as a distraction was serving her purpose
To suggest that a researcher's printed lists were flawed because they misrepresented a dialect's grammar
explanation: The setup line puts the focus on Ines. Across the excerpt she treats Aldo's stories as wasted time (she marks those minutes "as lost"). Then, after "however," she finds in one story four tenses her lists never asked about, and she switches to asking for more stories. So the excerpt shows her coming to see that the supposed distraction was actually giving her the data she came for. Choice C names the right person and the right change.

A.why: You moved the focus from Ines to Aldo and added a motive the text never gives. Aldo answers every prompt, just with stories, and the excerpt never mentions trust. This is the subtype's main trap: it uses the right characters but makes the wrong person the subject.

B.why: You saw that Ines changes her approach, which is the key insight, but you misread why. She puts the lists away because the stories gave her four tenses her lists missed. The change serves her research goals. It doesn't abandon them.

D.why: The text says the lists never thought to ask for certain tenses, so they were incomplete. It never says they contained errors or misrepresented the grammar. On top of that, the excerpt is about Ines's realization, not about judging her materials.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Teodor Lisk's 2016 poem "Annealing." The speaker addresses a young apprentice in a glassworks.

You flinch when the oven door shuts on your bowl,
as if the waiting were a verdict. It is not.
Glass that is hurried from fire into air
keeps the fire inside it as strain,
and one day breaks for no reason anyone can see.
So we cool it by hours, a degree at a time,
and what comes out looks no different—
only able, now, to be dropped and stay whole.
You are being cooled the same way. Let it take its time.
choices: To warn an apprentice that rushing her work will cause the glass she makes to crack and break
To explain the technical process by which glassmakers relieve the internal strain in their glass
To describe the speaker's lasting regret over the work she ruined when she was an apprentice
To reassure an apprentice that a period of waiting she dreads is what will make her resilient
explanation: The poem is addressed to the apprentice, so focus on what it says to her. She "flinch[es]" at the waiting, and the speaker answers right away: "It is not" a verdict. The description of slow cooling leads to the last line, "You are being cooled the same way," which turns the glass into a picture of her own slow training. Just as slow cooling makes the bowl able to "stay whole," the waiting she fears is making her stronger. The tone is comforting, which matches Choice D.

A.why: You noticed that hurried glass breaks, which is the key detail, but you finished the thought in the wrong tone. The apprentice isn't rushing anything. She is anxious about waiting, and the speaker calms her down ("It is not") instead of warning her. Turning an encouraging poem into a warning is this subtype's tone trap.

B.why: You described what most of the lines are about instead of what the poem does. The annealing process is there to set up the comparison in the last line about the apprentice. Someone who skipped that line could have written this choice, and that is a sign it misses the purpose.

C.why: The poem never mentions the speaker's own past failures or regrets. This choice invents a backstory and also moves the focus away from the apprentice the poem is speaking to.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Maren Halloway's 2009 novel The Long Exposure. Ruth, an amateur astronomer, has been photographing the night sky using her late father's observing notes.

Ruth had promised herself she would mail the plates to the observatory by Friday. The comet sat on the third plate exactly where her father's notebook said it would return, a smudge no wider than an eyelash. Once professionals confirmed it, the orbit would be printed in the catalog under his name, and the notebook would become a footnote. She slid the plate back into its sleeve, then took it out again, and held it to the window until the light went.
choices: To portray Ruth's pride that her father's long-ago prediction about the comet has finally proved correct
To convey Ruth's reluctance to give up something private even as she prepares to honor her father publicly
To illustrate the patience her father showed in tracking the comet's orbit across many years of observation
To suggest that Ruth has begun to doubt whether the smudge on the plate is really the returning comet
explanation: Your focus is Ruth. Mailing the plates will put her father's name in the catalog, which is a public honor. It will also turn his notebook, her private link to him, into 'a footnote.' She puts the plate away and then takes it out again, so she is putting off a step she has already promised to take. The excerpt as a whole shows her torn between honoring him and keeping something for herself.

A.why: You correctly saw that the father's prediction was confirmed, then assumed Ruth must feel proud. The text never names pride. Her actions after the confirmation show hesitation, and that is what the excerpt is built around.

C.why: You moved the focus from Ruth to her father. His notebook is the background. The excerpt is about what Ruth does with the plate, not about how he worked.

D.why: The comet sits 'exactly where' the notebook predicted, so Ruth has no reason to doubt it. You read her handling of the plate as uncertainty about the image. It is really hesitation about letting it go.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Tomás Eberle's 2014 memoir Drawn Lines. Early in his career, Eberle worked as a junior planner on a city's waterfront redesign.

On the drawings the new promenade was a clean gray ribbon, and I had drawn most of it. I was proudest of the gentle curve at the ferry landing; the director called it the best line in the set. Walking the site the week before demolition, I found that the curve passed directly over Mrs. Albescu's bench, where she had fed pigeons every morning for as long as anyone at the bakery could remember. I went back to the office and said nothing.
choices: To show the narrator's pride in a design feature that his director singled out for special praise
To criticize the director for approving a plan that ignored the daily routines of local residents
To recount the narrator's discovery that his best work carries a cost he chooses not to raise
To describe how Mrs. Albescu responded when she learned that her bench was to be removed
explanation: Sketch the order: pride in the curve, then the discovery that it erases Mrs. Albescu's bench, then silence. The excerpt is about the narrator. His proudest line costs something the neighborhood treasures, and he decides not to mention it. Only this choice covers both the discovery and the silence.

A.why: You stopped after the first two sentences. The pride is only the setup. The site visit overturns it, and a choice that leaves out the turn misses the purpose of the whole excerpt.

B.why: You moved the blame to the director. The director only praises the curve. The narrator drew it, found the problem, and kept quiet, so the excerpt is about him.

D.why: The text never says Mrs. Albescu learns anything or reacts. You filled in a scene the excerpt doesn't give.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Ada Krell's 1998 poem "For the Night Inspector." The speaker addresses a person who inspects a city bridge.

You walk the girders while the city sleeps,
tapping each rivet like a doctor's knuckle
against a chest, listening for the hollow note.
By morning you are gone. The buses cross,
the joggers cross, a boy with a kite crosses,
and none of them will think of you at all—
which is the whole of what you meant to build:
a day so ordinary no one thanks it.
choices: To warn the inspector that a flaw in the bridge could go unnoticed during a night inspection
To compare the inspector's careful work on the bridge to a doctor's examination of a patient
To lament that the inspector's careful labor goes unthanked by the people who depend on it
To honor the inspector by presenting the public's unawareness as proof of the work's success
explanation: The turn comes at the dash: people's forgetting the inspector is 'the whole of what you meant to build.' An ordinary day nobody thanks is the goal of the work, not an injustice. The speaker is paying tribute, and the people's unawareness is how the poem measures the inspector's success.

A.why: You treated 'listening for the hollow note' as a warning. Nothing in the poem suggests a flaw gets missed. The bridge carries everyone safely, and the tone is admiring, not anxious.

B.why: The doctor comparison is one simile in the second line. You chose an image the poem uses and treated it as the poem's purpose.

C.why: You correctly saw that no one thinks of the inspector, then read that as sad. The final lines say this unawareness is exactly what the inspector meant to build, so the tone is tribute, not lament.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Priya Venkataraman's 2017 novel Dry Season. Lakshmi, an agricultural scientist, is setting up trial plots of a drought-tolerant millet on her grandfather's farm.

Her grandfather watched her stake out the plots with string and numbered flags. He had planted by the first rains for sixty years, he said, and then he said it again. But when she knelt to log soil moisture, he brought the old brass probe from the shed, wiped it on his shirt, and asked her to show him where to write the number.
choices: To portray the grandfather's movement from wary skepticism toward a willingness to join her work
To show Lakshmi's determination to modernize the farm in spite of her grandfather's objections
To convey the grandfather's insistence that his way of planting is superior to scientific trials
To explain why the new variety of millet is expected to perform better in a dry growing season
explanation: The setup introduces Lakshmi, but the excerpt follows her grandfather. He starts out guarded and repeats his sixty years of planting by the rains. After 'But,' he brings his own tool and asks to record the data himself. The purpose is to show that change in him.

B.why: You kept the focus on Lakshmi because the setup names her. The excerpt describes what the grandfather does, and he never really objects. He only reminds her of his experience.

C.why: You read the first half and stopped. The 'But' turns the paragraph, and the grandfather ends up taking part in the trial rather than resisting it.

D.why: The excerpt never explains how or why the millet tolerates drought. You supplied a detail the text doesn't give.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Henrik Solberg's 2003 short story "Soundings." Ilse works in a coastal survey office, revising a nautical chart.

The new soundings moved the sandbar forty meters east. Ilse erased the old line carefully, as she had been taught, leaving no ghost of it on the vellum. Her predecessor had drawn that line in 1958, and three generations of captains had trusted it. She inked the new curve, checked it twice, and then, in pencil small enough to pass for a flaw in the paper, wrote his initials in the margin beside it.
choices: To show Ilse's reluctance to make a correction that will erase the work of her predecessor
To portray Ilse's quiet wish to acknowledge her predecessor while making a needed correction
To convey Ilse's disapproval of her predecessor for an error that misled many captains
To describe the procedures a survey office follows when it updates an existing chart
explanation: Ilse does the correction thoroughly. She erases the old line without a trace, inks the new curve, and checks it twice. Then she adds the predecessor's initials so small they could pass for a flaw in the paper. She does the job fully and still finds a private way to credit the man whose line she replaced.

A.why: You saw that Ilse respects her predecessor and assumed she must hesitate to correct him. She doesn't hesitate. She erases 'carefully, as she had been taught' and checks the new line twice. The respect comes after the correction, not instead of it.

C.why: Writing his initials beside the new line is a tribute, not a criticism. The captains 'trusted' the old line, and the text never says it misled them.

D.why: The procedural details are there, but they set up Ilse's private gesture. A choice about office procedure leaves out the character the excerpt is about.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from June Okafor's 2011 memoir The Reversed Image. Okafor recalls her first year as an apprentice in a woodcut studio.

My teacher pulled a proof from the block I had spent three weeks carving and laid it on the table without a word. The lines were clean; I had checked every one with a loupe. He turned the print upside down, then sideways, and at last said that the sky was well cut. Only that evening, scrubbing ink from the rollers, did I understand that he had said nothing about the birds, which were the reason I had made it.
choices: To show the teacher's approval of the precise technique his apprentice had worked to master
To depict the narrator's satisfaction with a print whose lines she had inspected so closely
To explain why the teacher judged the birds in the narrator's print to be poorly carved
To convey the narrator's delayed realization that narrow praise hid her teacher's disappointment
explanation: The key word is 'Only that evening.' The teacher praises one part, the sky, and says nothing about the birds, which mattered most to her. She works out later what that silence meant. The excerpt is about her coming to understand that the limited praise covered disappointment.

A.why: You took 'the sky was well cut' as approval and moved the focus to the teacher. The narrator later realizes the praise was a way of avoiding the part she cared about, so it isn't really approval.

B.why: Her confidence after checking with a loupe is only the starting point. The excerpt ends with that confidence undercut, and this choice leaves out the realization.

C.why: The teacher gives no reason and says nothing about the birds at all. You supplied a judgment the text leaves unspoken.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is adapted from Kenji Arai's 2020 novel The Quiet Interval. Noriko monitors instruments at a regional seismic station; her brother, Daisuke, lives in a town near a fault line.

At 3:12 the needle began to shiver, then to swing. Noriko read the amplitude, then the arrival times, and the numbers placed the epicenter well north of Hanase, where Daisuke lived. She typed the report in the prescribed order and sent it before she let herself reach for the phone. When he answered, sleepy and irritated, she asked him nothing about the earthquake, only whether he had fixed the gate.
choices: To convey Noriko's fear that the earthquake has struck the town where her brother lives
To illustrate the procedure a seismologist follows to locate the epicenter of an earthquake
To portray Noriko keeping her concern for her brother contained within routine and restraint
To show Daisuke's irritation at being woken by a sister who calls about household repairs
explanation: She files the report first and only then 'let herself' call, which shows she was holding back the urge. On the phone she asks about the gate, not the earthquake. The call shows she cares, and the ordinary question keeps that care hidden. The excerpt is about Noriko holding her worry inside routine.

A.why: You correctly sensed that Noriko is worried, then made the worry too specific. Her readings put the epicenter 'well north of Hanase,' so she knows the town wasn't hit.

B.why: The readings are background that sets up Noriko's restraint. A choice about technique leaves out the character and her brother.

D.why: You moved the focus to Daisuke. His irritation is a passing detail. The excerpt follows Noriko's choices.

stem: Which choice best states the main purpose of the text?
stimulus:
The following text is from Sofía Marend's 2015 poem "Field Recording." The speaker, a linguist, addresses an elderly woman who is the last fluent speaker of her language.

Say it again, the word for the river in spring—
the levels are right now; the red light holds.
The machine will keep your vowel, the small catch
before the final stop, exactly.
It will not keep the way you turned to the window
to find the word, as if the river told you,
or how you laughed when I said it back wrong.
Say it again. I am getting everything but you.
choices: To express the speaker's awareness that the recording can capture the woman's words but not her presence
To celebrate the recording's power to preserve the woman's language exactly as she speaks it
To urge the woman to speak more clearly so that the recording of her language will be accurate
To apologize to the woman for having mispronounced her word for the river in spring
explanation: The poem turns on 'will keep' versus 'will not keep.' The machine records the sounds exactly. It misses her turn toward the window and her laugh. The last line says it directly: 'everything but you.' The purpose is the speaker's recognition of what a recording cannot hold.

B.why: You saw that 'exactly' praises the machine and stopped there. The next three lines list what it cannot keep, and the closing line makes that loss the point of the poem.

C.why: 'Say it again' is a recording request, not a complaint about her speech. The speaker says the machine already gets her vowel 'exactly,' so clarity is never the problem.

D.why: The mispronunciation is one remembered moment, and it is offered as something precious, her laugh. You took an incidental detail for the poem's purpose.
